cards.headline: One currency, priced in another.
cards.body: This track is optional — useful to understand, not needed before you invest. Forex means trading currencies, always in pairs: euros priced in dollars, say. You are never buying one thing, but betting one currency against another.

art.alt: Two national coins balance on a small scale while a large lever beneath tips the whole platform far from a tiny nudge — small currency moves magnified by leverage.

cards.headline: A pip is the smallest step.
cards.body: Currency prices move in tiny increments called pips. For most pairs a pip is the fourth decimal place — **0.0001**. A move from 1.1000 to 1.1001 is one pip. Traders count gains and losses in pips before turning them into money.

cards.headline: A pip is worth more at size.
cards.body: What a pip pays depends on how much currency you hold. On a standard lot of 100,000 units, one pip is worth about **$10**. On a mini lot of 10,000 it is **$1**; on a micro lot of 1,000, just **$0.10**. Same pip, different stakes.

cards.title: Pip value by lot size
cards.caption: The same one-pip move pays ten dollars on a standard lot but a dime on a micro lot. Position size sets how much each tick is worth.

cards.headline: Pips are not percent.
cards.body: A hundred pips sounds big, but it is not one percent. A move from 1.1000 to 1.1100 is 100 pips, yet only **0.91%** — you divide the change by the price. Those small percentages are why forex traders reach for leverage.

cards.prompt: At 50:1 leverage, $2,000 controls $100,000. If the pair moves 2% against you, how much do you lose?
cards.explanation: Leverage sizes the loss off the $100,000, not your $2,000. A 2% move is **$2,000** — the entire margin. That is how a small price move wipes an account: the loss is measured against the borrowed size.

cards.headline: Leverage is the real risk.
cards.body: Because each percent is small, brokers offer huge leverage to make moves feel worthwhile. That same leverage means a tiny move against you erases the whole stake. In forex it is almost never the currency that ruins people. It is the borrowing.
Leverage sizes your loss off the full position, so a 2% move on a $100,000 position is [[1]], not 2% of your cash.
cards.explanation: Two percent of $100,000 is $2,000, regardless of how little of your own money is posted as margin. The borrowed size is what the percentage bites into — which is exactly why leverage magnifies losses.

cards.summary: Forex trades currency pairs in pips, where small percent moves are magnified by heavy leverage.
bullets: A pip is 0.0001; its value scales with lot size.
Leverage measures losses off the full position, not your cash.

art.alt: Two national coins balance on a small scale while a large lever beneath tips the whole platform far from a tiny nudge — small currency moves magnified by leverage.

cards.insight: Currencies barely move in percent, so forex sells you leverage to make it interesting. The leverage, not the currency, empties accounts.
